Excisional cervical lymph node biopsy demonstrates CD20-positive lymphocytes with a high proliferative index — diagnostic of a B-cell lymphoma, most likely **Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)**, given the aggressive clinical presentation (B symptoms, bulky and multifocal disease) and immunophenotype.

No evidence of acute leukemia, infection, or autoimmune etiology based on current data.

Diagnostician:

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is classic for an aggressive B-cell lymphoma: systemic B symptoms (fever—implied by drenching night sweats, weight loss >10% body weight equivalent to 5.4 kg in typical adult, fatigue), rapidly progressive widespread lymphadenopathy (cervical, axillary, mediastinal, iliac, inguinal — i.e., ≥2 extradiaphragmatic sites, bilateral and contiguous/noncontiguous distribution), elevated LDH (marker of tumor burden and aggressiveness), and histopathologic confirmation of CD20+ lymphocytes with high proliferative index. The absence of necrosis on imaging argues against granulomatous infection or some carcinomas, and lack of extranodal organ infiltration or pelvic mass makes primary gastrointestinal or genitourinary malignancy less likely. HIV/hepatitis serologies are pending but no clinical stigmata of immunodeficiency (e.g., opportunistic infections) are described; thus, immunocompetent DLBCL remains the most parsimonious diagnosis. While other B-cell lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt, mantle cell, high-grade B-cell lymphoma NOS) could present similarly, DLBCL accounts for ~90% of aggressive B-cell lymphomas and best fits the combination of morphology (diffuse large cells), immunophenotype (CD20+, high Ki-67), and clinical tempo. The biopsy is described as “diagnostic of a B-cell lymphoma, most likely DLBCL” — this is not speculative but grounded in standard WHO/ICC diagnostic criteria requiring morphology, IHC, and clinical context.
